segments.say: In eighteen forty three, the Danish philosopher Søren Kierkegaard published a book called Either Or. In one essay, written in the voice of a playful character, he described boredom as a kind of root of evil, and joked that the gods were bored, so they created human beings. And humans were bored, so they created more and more distractions.

Kierkegaard's essay was partly humorous, but it carried a serious point. He suggested that much of human restlessness, our constant seeking of novelty, entertainment and change, might come from trying to escape boredom. And he proposed a strange cure. Not more distraction, but a kind of creative use of limitation, finding interest in small things.

A few years earlier, the German philosopher Arthur Schopenhauer had written that human life swings like a pendulum between pain and boredom. When we lack something, we suffer from wanting it. When we have it, we soon become bored. In his rather gloomy view, boredom was one of the fundamental conditions of human existence.

Schopenhauer's view is quite pessimistic. But it captures something we've seen in modern psychology too. Remember the hedonic treadmill, where we quickly adapt to good things and start wanting more. Schopenhauer saw that pattern long before psychologists measured it. Satisfaction fades, and boredom creeps in.

In the twentieth century, the German philosopher Martin Heidegger wrote lectures on boredom, in which he distinguished different kinds. Being bored by something, like waiting for a train. Being bored with something, like an evening that was pleasant but somehow empty. And a deeper, profound boredom, where everything seems indifferent, and nothing grips us at all.

Heidegger suggested that this profound boredom, uncomfortable as it is, could reveal something important. When nothing grips us, we're confronted with the bare fact of our existence, and with the question of what we really want to do with our lives. In this view, deep boredom isn't just emptiness. It's a moment of potential awakening.

Even earlier, in the seventeenth century, the French thinker Blaise Pascal wrote a famous line in his Pensées. He suggested that all of humanity's problems stem from our inability to sit quietly in a room alone. Remember the shock study. Pascal might not have been surprised by those results at all.

What I find fascinating is how these old philosophical voices echo modern research. Pascal's quiet room, and people choosing shocks over stillness. Schopenhauer's pendulum, and the hedonic treadmill. Kierkegaard's restless search for distraction, and our phones. Heidegger's boredom as a signal, and boredom as a search for meaning.

These thinkers took boredom seriously. Not as a trivial annoyance, but as a window into the human condition. Into our restlessness, our desires, our need for meaning. And perhaps that's a good invitation for us. To treat our own boredom not just as something to escape, but as something to understand.

Tonight, you might be in a quiet room, alone, as Pascal described. And that's perfectly alright. You don't need to escape it. You can simply rest here, with your thoughts drifting softly, the way thoughts do when the world is still.

So here's what philosophers have said about boredom. Kierkegaard saw much of human restlessness as an escape from boredom. Schopenhauer described life as a pendulum between pain and boredom. Heidegger suggested that deep boredom could reveal what truly matters. And Pascal noted how hard it is for people to sit quietly in a room alone.

show.title: Philosophers of boredom
items: Kierkegaard saw restlessness as fleeing boredom
Schopenhauer: life swings between pain and boredom
Heidegger: deep boredom can reveal what matters
Pascal: we can't sit quietly in a room

segments.say: And long before these philosophers, there were monks in the deserts of Egypt who wrote vividly about a restless, weary feeling that struck around noon. Their descriptions sound remarkably modern. Let's visit them next.
